'''Chris Quigg''' (born December 15, 1944) is an [[Americans|American]] [[theoretical physicist]] at the [[Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory]] (Fermilab).  He graduated from Yale University in 1966 and received his Ph.D. in 1970 under the tutelage of [[John David Jackson (physicist)|J. D. Jackson]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].  He has been an associate professor at the Institute for Theoretical Physics, [[State University of New York, Stony Brook]], and was head of the Theoretical Physics Department at Fermilab from 1977 to 1987.

==Contributions to physics==
Quigg's contributions range over many topics in particle physics.  With [[Benjamin W. Lee|Benjamin Lee]] and [[H. B. Thacker]] in 1977 he identified the uppermost theoretical mass scale for the [[Higgs boson]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Benjamin W. Lee |author2=C. Quigg |author3=H. B. Thacker | title=Strength of Weak Interactions at Very High Energies and the Higgs Boson Mass | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=38 | issue=16 | pages=883–885 | year=1977 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.38.883 | bibcode=1977PhRvL..38..883L}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Benjamin W. Lee |author2=C. Quigg |author3=H. B. Thacker | title=Weak interactions at very high energies: The role of the Higgs-boson mass | journal=Physical Review | volume=D16 | issue=5 | pages=1519–1531 | year=1977 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.16.1519|bibcode = 1977PhRvD..16.1519L }}</ref>  In 1984 he coauthored "Supercollider Physics" (with [[Estia Eichten]], [[Kenneth Lane (physicist)|Kenneth Lane]] and [[Ian Hinchliffe]]), which has strongly influenced the quest for future discoveries at hadron colliders, such as the Fermilab [[Tevatron]], the [[Superconducting Super Collider|SSC]], and the [[Large Hadron Collider|LHC]] at [[CERN]].<ref>{{cite journal |author1=E. Eichten |author2=I. Hinchliffe |author3=K. Lane |author4=C. Quigg | title=Supercollider Physics | journal=Reviews of Modern Physics | volume=56 | issue=4 | pages=579–707 | year=1984 | doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.56.579 | bibcode=1984RvMP...56..579E}}</ref>  He is also author of ''Gauge Theories of the Strong, Weak, and Electromagnetic Interactions''.<ref>{{cite book | author=Chris Quigg | title=Gauge Theories of the Strong, Weak, and Electromagnetic Interactions | publisher=Westview Press | series=Advanced Book Classics | year=1997 | isbn=978-0-201-32832-5}}</ref>

He has made many other significant contributions to the study of the spectroscopy of heavy-light mesons, signatures for the production of heavy quarks and quarkonium, and the study of ultrahigh-energy neutrino interactions.  He is an international lecturer and public speaker, and has been Editor of the ''[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science]]''.

{{blockquote|He was a consultant to [[WQED (TV)|WQED]] and the National Academy of Sciences for the ''Infinite Voyage'' television series and a featured speaker in the companion Discovery Lectures on college campuses. He gave the first Carl Sagan Memorial Lecture in the series ''Cosmos Revisited'' at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. He was featured in ''The Ultimate Particle'', a road movie of particle physics broadcast on [[Arte|ARTE]] in France and Germany.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chris Quigg, Brief Biography|website=lutece.fnal.gov, Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory|url=https://lutece.fnal.gov/Essays/Bio2.html}}</ref>}}

With Robert N. Cahn, he wrote ''Grace in All Simplicity'', subtitled "Beauty, Truth, and Wonders on the Path to the Higgs Boson and New Laws of Naturea", a popular book on the history and development of the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics,

==Awards and honors==
Quigg was a recipient of the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] Research Fellowship, 1974–1978, and was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1983. In 2011 Quigg with [[Estia Eichten]], [[Ian Hinchliffe]], and [[Kenneth Lane (physicist)|Kenneth Lane]] won the [[Sakurai Prize|J. J. Sakurai Prize for Theoretical Particle Physics]] ''"For their work, separately and collectively, to chart a course of the exploration of TeV scale physics using multi-TeV hadron colliders"'' <ref>[http://www.aps.org/units/dpf/awards/sakurai.cfm American Physical Society - J. J. Sakurai Prize Winners]</ref>
